content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the critical importance of quality assurance (QA) in the use of HIV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), particularly in the context of antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation based solely on HIV serological diagnosis. HIV testing at the point of care is a vital component of prevention efforts and serves as a key entry point into the HIV care and treatment cascade. WHO supports the use of RDTs within validated national HIV testing algorithms and encourages their use by non-laboratory healthcare personnel and lay providers to expand HIV testing services, prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), and improve access to care and treatment. Both false-positive and false-negative results have been reported across various programs and countries, raising concerns about individuals being incorrectly diagnosed as HIV-positive and unnecessarily starting lifelong ART. This issue is particularly concerning in settings where ART is initiated based solely on HIV serological diagnosis, such as under the Option B+ approach and for children under five years of age. Retesting prior to ART initiation is also advised to verify HIV-positive diagnoses, although retesting individuals already on ART is not recommended. The consequences of misdiagnosis are significant. False-positive diagnoses can lead to unnecessary ART initiation, exposing individuals to potential side effects, stigma, and psychological stress, while false-negative diagnoses result in missed opportunities for timely treatment and ongoing transmission risks. These issues are exacerbated in low-prevalence settings, where the positive predictive value of HIV testing decreases. WHO highlights the need for national programs to develop and adhere to validated testing algorithms tailored to the prevalence of HIV in their settings. A positive HIV status should only be confirmed after two sequential reactive test results in high-prevalence settings (≥5%) or three sequential reactive results in low-prevalence settings (<5%). Strict adherence to these algorithms is essential to minimize the risk of misdiagnosis. Countries like Malawi, which pioneered the PMTCT Option B+ approach, have implemented systematic retesting as part of their national guidelines, demonstrating its feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Economic evaluations suggest that the cost of retesting is significantly lower than the lifetime treatment costs associated with false-positive diagnoses. For example, the lifetime cost of ART for an individual is estimated at $17,570, while the cost of retesting ranges from $5 to $20 per person. Retesting not only prevents unnecessary treatment costs but also reinforces public confidence in HIV testing services. To further improve QA, WHO recommends the use of innovative tools such as smartphone-based RDT readers, which can enhance the accuracy of test result interpretation. Additionally, community-based volunteers, known as Quality Corps (Q-Corps), are being piloted in some countries to support QA activities at decentralized testing sites. These volunteers assist with logistics, data analysis, site assessments, and follow-up on QA implementation. In conclusion, QA activities are essential at every HIV testing site. Ministries of Health and national HIV programs must prioritize QA and quality improvement efforts, ensuring that national policies, guidelines, and training curricula incorporate best practices. This is particularly important in clinical settings implementing WHO's 2013 Consolidated ARV Guidelines, which recommend ART initiation based solely on HIV serological diagnosis.
